messages.speaker: me
messages.text: finished part one tonight and had to sit in the stairwell for a while. no spoilers about the lighthouse

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: The stairwell is the right reading room for that one. Part one ends the way a tide goes out — you're left standing further from shore than you were, without quite knowing how you got there

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: the ledger-counting scene did it to me

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: That counting is the first time the prose drops its mask. Until then he is performing composure for the reader; the recitation is him speaking to the only listener he still trusts, which is repetition itself

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: repetition itself. the club notes missed all of this by a mile

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Of course they did — club notes are built for plot traffic, not for what the sentences are doing. Saved for later: does the second part keep the present tense, or does time finally move?

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: present tense holds, except in the letters, which go past. it wrecks your sense of when anything is happening

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: That's the device working, not failing. The letters are the only place he permits a completed past — which tells you exactly where his grief lives

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: right. do i read on tonight or sit with part one for a day first

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Read on. The second part rewards momentum more than reverence, and its closing page does to the lighthouse what part one did to the tide

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: i'll report back from the stairwell

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Report from wherever you like — though ring my bell rather than messaging late. Tuesdays and thursdays i'm at my sister's until ten

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: I've started a margin page for you — the appendices cross-reference the ledger entries in ways the club edition cuts entirely. It'll be finished by the weekend

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: take your time. also: the letter on page 208 rearranged my whole reading of the marriage

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Then the book is doing its work in you. The marriage only becomes legible once you notice she is the sole addressee left in the surviving letters — every other name in the ledger is a transaction

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: every other name is a transaction. that's the sentence the club needs

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Come to the next one and say it aloud. People polite-argue with printed notes; they rarely know what to do with an actual reading

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: only if you're there to back me up

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: I sit two armchairs from the kettle, you can't miss me. Bring page flags this time — you dog-ear like someone punishing the book for being good

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: the dog-ears are a love language. tuesday then

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Tuesday. I'll make the coffee before you ask — instant is a compromise, but it's the compromise we've lived with since 2019

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: deal. and no spoilers from the appendices

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Margin notes are commentary, not prophecy. Though i will admit the appendix on the keepers' rota re-rigged the final chapter for me entirely

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: now saturday feels very far away

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: It always does, eventually. That's the one mercy no appendix can take from us

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: I finished the margin page for your loan — and i hear from the stairwell hour that you've finished the book. Tell me the ending did what the letters promised

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: it did. the whole ending is a reallocation — everything he counted turns out to be a debt

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Then you've read it right. Nothing resolves; the debts are settled in daylight he never knew was owned. And the niece's silence at the close is deliberate, not an accident of the cutting

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: the silence as the last kindness. i kept waiting for a reveal

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Everyone the ledger touches ends up keeping the lighthouse in some way. The book is quietly refusing to appoint her

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: who has to carry what — that's the whole thesis

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Yes, plus its corollary: carrying can be inherited by accident. Save that one for tuesday, it starts the argument you'll want

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: and the appendices will be waiting on your hall table?

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: With the margin page clipped on top. Mind my margins — the shorthand around the rota section defeats even me

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: one thing i couldn't crack: does the niece ever actually see the third ledger?

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: No — and the withholding is the last mercy in it. Anyone who reads the third ledger starts keeping something; hers is the one inheritance the book refuses to arrange

messages.speaker: me
messages.text: the club is getting two arguments on tuesday then, you realise

messages.speaker: them
messages.text: Two is modest. I'm bringing the rota shorthand as a third — see you tuesday
